entities.summary:
Robert Briçonnet (c. 1450 – 12 June 1497) was a prominent French prelate and statesman who rose to become Archbishop of Reims, playing a significant role in the ecclesiastical and political landscape of late 15th-century France. Hailing from the influential Briçonnet family, a powerful dynastic force in Touraine, his career spanned pivotal moments during the reigns of Louis XI and Charles VIII. He epitomized the intersection of clerical ambition and royal service, leveraging his familial connections and intellectual acumen to secure high office and contribute to the administrative machinery of the Valois monarchy, particularly during a period of consolidation following the Hundred Years' War.

Briçonnet's ascent began with his appointment as Canon of Tours and Archdeacon of Reims, positions that provided a foundation for his later ecclesiastical achievements. His political influence was cemented through his close ties to the royal court, serving as a trusted counselor to King Charles VIII. He notably participated in the Estates General of Tours in 1484, a critical assembly that debated royal authority and financial policy in the wake of Louis XI's death. His elevation to Bishop of Saint-Malo in 1486, followed by his appointment as Archbishop of Reims in 1493, placed him at the apex of the French Church, granting him considerable spiritual and temporal power, including the traditional right to crown French monarchs.
